fullDescription.text: A local variable (VAR, VAR_TEMP, VAR_STAT, VAR_INST) is declared but never read or written by any code, initial value or declaration in the project.

help.text: A local variable (VAR, VAR_TEMP, VAR_STAT, VAR_INST) is declared but never read or written by any code, initial value or declaration in the project.
help.markdown:
## Description

A local variable (VAR, VAR_TEMP, VAR_STAT, VAR_INST) is declared but never read or written by any code, initial
value or declaration in the project.

## Rationale

Unused declarations make a POU harder to read and suggest unfinished or dead logic; they also use memory. PLCopen
Coding Guidelines rule CP24 *Do not declare variables that are not used*.

Not reported, because something outside the parsed code may use the variable: variables with an attribute pragma
(HMI, OPC UA or ADS exposure), variables with an `AT` address (I/O mapping), names matching `sparePattern`, and every
variable of a POU with a graphical or unparsable body. Inputs and outputs are interface, not locals, and are not
checked here.

## Noncompliant

```st
FUNCTION_BLOCK FB_Pump
VAR_INPUT
    bStart : BOOL;
END_VAR
VAR
    bRunning : BOOL;
    nOldCounter : INT;
END_VAR
bRunning := bStart;
END_FUNCTION_BLOCK
```

## Compliant

```st
FUNCTION_BLOCK FB_Pump
VAR_INPUT
    bStart : BOOL;
END_VAR
VAR
    bRunning : BOOL;
    nSpare1 : INT;
END_VAR
bRunning := bStart;
END_FUNCTION_BLOCK
```

fullDescription.text: A CASE statement has no ELSE branch, so an unexpected selector value silently does nothing.

help.text: A CASE statement has no ELSE branch, so an unexpected selector value silently does nothing.
help.markdown:
## Description

A CASE statement has no ELSE branch, so an unexpected selector value silently does nothing.

## Rationale

State machines are usually written as CASE statements. If the state variable takes a value no branch handles (a new
state, a corrupted value, a bad HMI write), the machine stops in an undefined state without any alarm. An ELSE branch
makes that case explicit: raise an error or go to a safe state. PLCopen rule L17 asks the same for IF; the guidelines
have no CASE rule, so no PLCopen id is given.

A CASE on an enumeration that handles every value is not reported by default.

## Noncompliant

```st
PROGRAM P_Sequence
VAR
    nStep : INT;
END_VAR
CASE nStep OF
    0: nStep := 10;
    10: nStep := 0;
END_CASE
END_PROGRAM
```

## Compliant

```st
PROGRAM P_Sequence
VAR
    nStep : INT;
    bFault : BOOL;
END_VAR
CASE nStep OF
    0: nStep := 10;
    10: nStep := 0;
ELSE
    bFault := TRUE;
END_CASE
END_PROGRAM
```

fullDescription.text: A REAL or LREAL value is compared with `=` or `<>`.

help.text: A REAL or LREAL value is compared with `=` or `<>`.
help.markdown:
## Description

A REAL or LREAL value is compared with `=` or `<>`.

## Rationale

Floating-point values carry rounding errors, so a computed value is rarely exactly equal to another; the comparison
may never become TRUE (a sequence that never advances) or flicker. Compare the difference against a tolerance
instead. PLCopen Coding Guidelines rule CP8 *Floating point comparison shall not be equality or inequality*.

## Noncompliant

```st
FUNCTION F_AtTarget : BOOL
VAR_INPUT
    rPosition : REAL;
    rTarget : REAL;
END_VAR
F_AtTarget := rPosition = rTarget;
END_FUNCTION
```

## Compliant

```st
FUNCTION F_AtTarget : BOOL
VAR_INPUT
    rPosition : REAL;
    rTarget : REAL;
END_VAR
F_AtTarget := ABS(rPosition - rTarget) < 0.001;
END_FUNCTION
```

fullDescription.text: The divisor of `/`, `MOD`, `DIV(…)` or `MOD(…)` is a literal or constant that evaluates to zero.

help.text: The divisor of `/`, `MOD`, `DIV(…)` or `MOD(…)` is a literal or constant that evaluates to zero.
help.markdown:
## Description

The divisor of `/`, `MOD`, `DIV(…)` or `MOD(…)` is a literal or constant that evaluates to zero.

## Rationale

An integer division by zero raises an exception on most runtimes and stops the PLC; a REAL division yields infinity
or NaN that spreads through the calculation. A divisor that is always zero is a bug, often a constant that was
changed or not yet set.

## Noncompliant

```st
FUNCTION F_Average : INT
VAR_INPUT
    nSum : INT;
END_VAR
VAR CONSTANT
    cSamples : INT := 0;
END_VAR
F_Average := nSum / cSamples;
END_FUNCTION
```

## Compliant

```st
FUNCTION F_Average : INT
VAR_INPUT
    nSum : INT;
END_VAR
VAR CONSTANT
    cSamples : INT := 8;
END_VAR
F_Average := nSum / cSamples;
END_FUNCTION
```

shortDescription.text: FOR loop variable modified in the loop body

fullDescription.text: The control variable of a FOR loop is assigned inside the loop body, passed to an output or VAR_IN_OUT parameter, or reused as the control variable of a nested FOR.

help.text: The control variable of a FOR loop is assigned inside the loop body, passed to an output or VAR_IN_OUT parameter, or reused as the control variable of a nested FOR.
help.markdown:
## Description

The control variable of a FOR loop is assigned inside the loop body, passed to an output or VAR_IN_OUT parameter, or
reused as the control variable of a nested FOR.

## Rationale

IEC 61131-3 says the control variable shall not be altered by the repeated statements. Changing it makes the number
of iterations unpredictable and can cause an endless loop, which trips the task watchdog. Use WHILE or REPEAT when
the iteration count is not known in advance. PLCopen Coding Guidelines rule *Loop variables should not be modified
inside a FOR loop*: the rule section says L12, the document's table of contents says L22.

## Noncompliant

```st
FUNCTION F_FindFirst : INT
VAR_INPUT
    aValues : ARRAY[1..10] OF INT;
END_VAR
VAR
    i : INT;
END_VAR
F_FindFirst := 0;
FOR i := 1 TO 10 DO
    IF aValues[i] > 0 THEN
        F_FindFirst := i;
        i := 10;
    END_IF
END_FOR
END_FUNCTION
```

## Compliant

```st
FUNCTION F_FindFirst : INT
VAR_INPUT
    aValues : ARRAY[1..10] OF INT;
END_VAR
VAR
    i : INT;
END_VAR
F_FindFirst := 0;
FOR i := 1 TO 10 DO
    IF aValues[i] > 0 THEN
        F_FindFirst := i;
        EXIT;
    END_IF
END_FOR
END_FUNCTION
```

fullDescription.text: A VAR_INPUT of a function, function block or method is written inside that POU (or a method or action of it).

help.text: A VAR_INPUT of a function, function block or method is written inside that POU (or a method or action of it).
help.markdown:
## Description

A VAR_INPUT of a function, function block or method is written inside that POU (or a method or action of it).

## Rationale

Inputs are set by the caller on every call. Overwriting one inside the POU hides the caller's value, and the effect
depends on whether the caller passes the input on the next call; for function blocks the changed value can also be
read back from outside. Copy the input to a local variable and change that. PLCopen Coding Guidelines rule CP17
*Usage of parameters shall match their declaration mode* ("each input parameter should not be written"). Writes
through a POINTER or REFERENCE input change the caller's data and are not reported.

## Noncompliant

```st
FUNCTION_BLOCK FB_Scale
VAR_INPUT
    rRaw : REAL;
END_VAR
VAR_OUTPUT
    rScaled : REAL;
END_VAR
IF rRaw < 0.0 THEN
    rRaw := 0.0;
END_IF
rScaled := rRaw * 0.1;
END_FUNCTION_BLOCK
```

## Compliant

```st
FUNCTION_BLOCK FB_Scale
VAR_INPUT
    rRaw : REAL;
END_VAR
VAR_OUTPUT
    rScaled : REAL;
END_VAR
VAR
    rClamped : REAL;
END_VAR
rClamped := MAX(rRaw, 0.0);
rScaled := rClamped * 0.1;
END_FUNCTION_BLOCK
```

fullDescription.text: A POU calls itself, directly or through a chain of other POUs (functions, methods, actions, FB bodies, property accessors).

help.text: A POU calls itself, directly or through a chain of other POUs (functions, methods, actions, FB bodies, property accessors).
help.markdown:
## Description

A POU calls itself, directly or through a chain of other POUs (functions, methods, actions, FB bodies, property
accessors).

## Rationale

Each recursive call uses stack space, and PLC stacks are small and fixed; deep recursion can stop the controller.
Support for recursion also differs between vendors, so the code is less portable. Replace the recursion with a loop.
PLCopen Coding Guidelines rule CP13 *POUs shall not call themselves directly or indirectly*.

## Noncompliant

```st
FUNCTION F_Factorial : DINT
VAR_INPUT
    n : DINT;
END_VAR
IF n <= 1 THEN
    F_Factorial := 1;
ELSE
    F_Factorial := n * F_Factorial(n - 1);
END_IF
END_FUNCTION
```

## Compliant

```st
FUNCTION F_Factorial : DINT
VAR_INPUT
    n : DINT;
END_VAR
VAR
    i : DINT;
END_VAR
F_Factorial := 1;
FOR i := 2 TO n DO
    F_Factorial := F_Factorial * i;
END_FOR
END_FUNCTION
```

fullDescription.text: An output-like variable — a physical output (`AT %Q…`), a global variable, or the POU's own VAR_OUTPUT — is written unconditionally in more than one place, so only the last write of each cycle takes effect.

help.text: An output-like variable — a physical output (`AT %Q…`), a global variable, or the POU's own VAR_OUTPUT — is written unconditionally in more than one place, so only the last write of each cycle takes effect.
help.markdown:
## Description

An output-like variable — a physical output (`AT %Q…`), a global variable, or the POU's own VAR_OUTPUT — is written
unconditionally in more than one place, so only the last write of each cycle takes effect.

## Rationale

This is the structured-text form of the ladder "double coil": two rungs driving the same coil. The earlier write is
dead, the behaviour depends on execution order, and the logic that decides the output is spread over the
application. Compute the value once, in one place. PLCopen Coding Guidelines rule CP12 *Physical outputs shall be
written once per PLC cycle* covers physical outputs; this rule also checks globals and FB outputs.

To stay quiet on correct code, only unconditional writes count (`:=` or `=>` in a top-level statement of a body),
`S=`/`R=` latches, read-modify-write statements (`n := n + 1`) and writes inside IF/CASE/loops are ignored, and a
second write in the same body is not reported when the variable is read in between (sequential use of a working
variable).

## Noncompliant

```st
PROGRAM P_Conveyor
VAR
    bStart : BOOL;
    bJog : BOOL;
    qMotor AT %QX0.0 : BOOL;
END_VAR
qMotor := bStart;
qMotor := bJog;
END_PROGRAM
```

## Compliant

```st
PROGRAM P_Conveyor
VAR
    bStart : BOOL;
    bJog : BOOL;
    qMotor AT %QX0.0 : BOOL;
END_VAR
qMotor := bStart OR bJog;
END_PROGRAM
```

fullDescription.text: A direct address such as `%IX0.1`, `%QW4` or `%MD10` is used in code instead of a symbolic variable.

help.text: A direct address such as `%IX0.1`, `%QW4` or `%MD10` is used in code instead of a symbolic variable.
help.markdown:
## Description

A direct address such as `%IX0.1`, `%QW4` or `%MD10` is used in code instead of a symbolic variable.

## Rationale

A bare address says nothing about what it is, makes the code depend on one hardware layout, and is easily missed when
the I/O configuration changes. Declare a variable with `AT %…` once and use its name. PLCopen Coding Guidelines rule
N1 *Avoid physical addresses*.

## Noncompliant

```st
PROGRAM P_Lamp
%QX0.1 := %IX0.0;
END_PROGRAM
```

## Compliant

```st
PROGRAM P_Lamp
VAR
    iButton AT %IX0.0 : BOOL;
    qLamp AT %QX0.1 : BOOL;
END_VAR
qLamp := iButton;
END_PROGRAM
```

fullDescription.text: A string literal is used as a password, token or other secret (assigned to, initialising, passed as or compared with a variable or parameter whose name matches `namePattern`), or a string literal is an IPv4 address.

help.text: A string literal is used as a password, token or other secret (assigned to, initialising, passed as or compared with a variable or parameter whose name matches `namePattern`), or a string literal is an IPv4 address.
help.markdown:
## Description

A string literal is used as a password, token or other secret (assigned to, initialising, passed as or compared with
a variable or parameter whose name matches `namePattern`), or a string literal is an IPv4 address.

## Rationale

Credentials in the PLC program are visible to anyone who can read the project or upload it from the controller,
cannot be rotated without a program change, and are often identical across machines. A password check against a
literal is a back door. Hard-coded IP addresses tie the program to one network layout and hide communication
partners from reviews. Keep secrets in a protected store and network settings in configuration.

## Noncompliant

```st
FUNCTION_BLOCK FB_Login
VAR_INPUT
    sUser : STRING;
    sPassword : STRING;
END_VAR
VAR_OUTPUT
    bAuthorized : BOOL;
END_VAR
VAR
    sServerIp : STRING := '192.168.10.20';
END_VAR
bAuthorized := sUser = 'service' AND sPassword = 'Service#2024';
END_FUNCTION_BLOCK
```

## Compliant

```st
FUNCTION_BLOCK FB_Login
VAR_INPUT
    sUser : STRING;
    sPassword : STRING;
    sExpectedHash : STRING;
END_VAR
VAR_OUTPUT
    bAuthorized : BOOL;
END_VAR
bAuthorized := F_Hash(sPassword) = sExpectedHash;
END_FUNCTION_BLOCK
```
